claims.claim: Thalidomide went on sale nationwide in West Germany as Contergan from 1 October 1957.
claims.episode_span: In October 1957, the German firm Chemie Grünenthal began selling thalidomide across West Germany under the name Contergan
claims.source_title: The Thalidomide tragedy | Thalidomide Website Grünenthal
claims.supporting_quote: From 1 October 1957, the drug was available in Germany nationwide – initially as a tablet, later also as a suppository and syrup.

claims.claim: Widukind Lenz warned Chemie Grünenthal by telephone in mid-November 1961 that thalidomide was the likely cause of the malformations (Lenz's own published account dates the call 16 November; Grünenthal's timeline records 15 November).
claims.episode_span: German pediatrician Widukind Lenz warned Grünenthal by telephone on 16 November 1961 that the drug was the likely cause
claims.source_title: The Thalidomide tragedy | Thalidomide Website Grünenthal
claims.supporting_quote: Events unfolded rapidly: 15 November 1961: Lenz informs Grünenthal of his suspicions. 20 November 1961: Grünenthal employees travel to Hamburg to speak with Lenz and the local health authorities in person.

claims.claim: William McBride's letter 'Thalidomide and Congenital Abnormalities' was published in The Lancet on 16 December 1961 (vol. 2, p. 1358).
claims.episode_span: the first published connection was a letter in The Lancet on 16 December 1961 from Australian obstetrician William McBride
claims.supporting_quote: "Thalidomide and Congenital Abnormalities." Letter to the Editor. The Lancet 2 (December 16, 1961): 1358.

claims.claim: More than 10,000 children worldwide were born with severe thalidomide-induced deformities such as phocomelia, alongside thousands of miscarriages.
claims.episode_span: roughly ten thousand children worldwide were born with thalidomide-induced malformations
claims.supporting_quote: more than 10,000 children born with a range of severe deformities, such as phocomelia , as well as thousands of miscarriages.

claims.claim: Grünenthal withdrew Contergan from the German market on 27 November 1961 and notified its international partners.
claims.episode_span: Grünenthal withdrew Contergan in November 1961; most other markets followed within months.
claims.source_title: The Thalidomide tragedy | Thalidomide Website Grünenthal
claims.supporting_quote: 27 November 1961: Grünenthal withdraws Contergan from the market and also informs its international distribution partners and licensees of this decision.

claims.claim: FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey withheld US approval of thalidomide, withstanding pressure from applicant Richardson-Merrell.
claims.episode_span: reviewer Frances Kelsey repeatedly requested additional safety data, citing the emerging neuritis reports
claims.supporting_quote: The refusal was largely due to pharmacologist Frances Oldham Kelsey , who withstood pressure from the Richardson-Merrell Pharmaceuticals Co.

claims.claim: The thalidomide disaster prompted tougher drug-testing laws, including the US Kefauver-Harris Amendment of 1962.
claims.episode_span: The episode prompted passage of the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which required proof of efficacy and more rigorous safety testing
claims.supporting_quote: The disaster prompted many countries to introduce tougher rules for the testing and licensing of drugs, such as the Kefauver Harris Amendment
